title: The stick in the baby's throat
hook: he says what is true and helpful even when unwelcome, at the right time, as you'd pull a stick from a baby's throat (MN 58)

segments.voice: Yesterday: subhasita vaca, well-spoken speech, with time first among its five marks. Your line: true, timely, kind.

A prince named Abhaya comes to the Buddha with a trick question someone has coached him to ask. It's built with two prongs, so that either answer sticks in the throat. Would you ever say something that others find unwelcome and disagreeable? If the Buddha says yes, how is he different from anyone else who hurts people's feelings? If he says no, what about the hard things he has said about the monk Devadatta? Abhaya sits down with his baby son on his lap. That small detail turns out to be the whole answer.
screen: `A TRICK QUESTION, TWO PRONGS.` → `YES OR NO, IT STICKS.` → `A BABY ON HIS LAP.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't say yes or no. He looks at the baby. Prince, he asks, if this child, through someone's carelessness, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? Abhaya answers at once. I'd get it out. If I couldn't get it out right away, I'd hold his head with my left hand, crook a finger of my right, and pull it out, even if it drew blood. Why? Because I have compassion for the child. That, the Buddha says, is how he speaks. Then he lays out the cases, six of them, like a grid. If something is untrue, or true but of no help, he doesn't say it, whether people would welcome it or not. If it's true and helpful but unwelcome, he knows the right time to say it. If it's true, helpful and welcome, again, he knows the right time. Look at what does the deciding. Whether people will like it is on the grid, but it never settles anything. Wounding them isn't on it at all. The deciding questions are: is it true, does it help? And then: when? Pulling a stick from a child's throat isn't gentle in the moment. There may be crying, even a little blood. But nobody watching would call it cruel, because everyone can see what it's for and who it's for. The sutta ends with Abhaya, who came to trap the Buddha, going for refuge instead. Some sticks come out easily.
screen: `HE LOOKS AT THE BABY.` · `I'D GET IT OUT, EVEN WITH BLOOD.` · `SIX CASES: TRUE, HELPFUL, WHEN.` · `WELCOME NEVER DECIDES.` · then, large: `THE RIGHT TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of one true thing someone in your life may need to hear, about their health, their work, a habit that's hurting them, and ask the Buddha's questions: is it true, will it help them, and then the hardest one, when? Picture a moment that would be right, when they can hear it, not when you're angry or tired, and picture your hand steady and careful, the way you'd reach for a child. Rest there with the breath.
Kala, time. The Buddha's picture for a truth that's unwelcome but needed: said for the other's sake, at the right time.
Your line: the right time. A needed truth waits for a moment they can hear it, and if that moment isn't today, waiting counts too. Go gently.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell this story when explaining right speech, and monastic communities have a formal way of pointing out a fellow monastic's fault, raised respectfully and at a suitable time.

what a scholar hears: MN 58 sorts speech into six cases by true or false, helpful or not, welcome or not; only the two true-and-helpful cases are spoken, and both turn on timing.

chat.says: Did the Buddha ever say things people didn't want to hear?
options: Yes, if true and helpful, at the right time, like a stick pulled from a baby's throat.
Never; he only said things that every listener would welcome and enjoy.
Yes, whenever something was true, whether or not it would help anyone.
chat.meaning: In MN 58, unwelcome words that are true and helpful are said at the right time, out of compassion, as a father pulls a stick from his child's throat.

Abhaya.meaning: a prince who came with a two-pronged trick question

Devadatta.meaning: a monk the Buddha had said hard things about

notes: MN 58 paraphrased. In the sutta Abhaya is sent by Nigantha Nataputta, the Jain teacher, to pose the two-pronged question (likened in the text to an iron spike stuck in the throat). The script says only 'someone has coached him' to avoid casting another tradition as a foil; Keeper may prefer naming him.
Devadatta: the Buddha had said Devadatta was bound for a state of deprivation; script says only 'the hard things he has said about Devadatta'.
Six cases summarized from the sutta; please confirm.
The original-language note uses kāla (time); the sutta's phrase is reportedly kālaññū (knowing the time): confirm before using the compound.
howItsDone mentions the monastic procedure of admonition (e.g. as described in the Vinaya and AN 5.167); confirm phrasing.

Editor review: 'Pleasing people isn't on the grid' was inaccurate (welcome/unwelcome is one axis of MN 58's six cases; it just never decides), now corrected in teach, screen head and myth reveal; dropped 'the cousin trying to split the community', which is from the Vinaya and commentary, not MN 58; 'while nobody was watching' now follows the sutta's 'through negligence'.
